title: Who Is Quietly Discipling You? The Invisible Voices That Can Either Draw You Closer to Christ—or Pull You Away Forever
paragraphs:
Who Is Quietly Discipling You? The Invisible Voices That Can Either Draw You Closer to Christ—or Pull You Away Forever
The people you admire today are shaping the person you will become tomorrow. The question is not whether you are being influenced—but whether that influence is leading you toward Jesus Christ or away from Him.
You probably didn't wake up this morning intending to drift away from God.
Very few Christians ever do.
No one plans to love Jesus less.
No one plans to compromise.
No one plans to slowly become numb to conviction.
It happens quietly.
One voice at a time.
One conversation at a time.
One influencer.
One podcast.
One television series.
One social media account.
One friendship.
One relationship.
One compromise that didn't seem dangerous enough to notice.
Before long, the heart that once burned for Christ becomes strangely comfortable with things that once brought tears of repentance.
That is why Scripture repeatedly warns believers to be vigilant—not only about what they believe, but about who is shaping what they believe.
Influence is discipleship.
Whether we realize it or not, every voice we repeatedly welcome into our lives is teaching us how to think, how to feel, what to love, what to fear, what to pursue, and ultimately whom to worship.
Jesus never asked only what enters your ears.
He asked what enters your heart.
The Apostle Paul wrote one of the simplest yet most devastating warnings found anywhere in Scripture:
"Do not be deceived: 'Bad company corrupts good morals.'" (1 Corinthians 15:33)
The Greek text reads:
Μὴ πλανᾶσθε· φθείρουσιν ἤθη χρηστὰ ὁμιλίαι κακαί.
Mē planasthe; phtheirousin ēthē chrēsta homiliai kakai.
The opening phrase Μὴ πλανᾶσθε (Mē planasthe) literally means:
"Stop allowing yourselves to be led astray."
The verb carries the idea of wandering from truth because someone or something has deceived you.
Paul assumes deception is already trying to happen.
Influence is rarely announced.
It usually arrives disguised as entertainment.
As success.
As humor.
As romance.
As acceptance.
As "just being open-minded."
As "living your truth."
As "everyone else is doing it."
That is how spiritual erosion begins.
Long before Israel worshiped golden calves, they listened to foreign voices.
Long before Solomon's heart turned away from God, he welcomed relationships that slowly redirected his affections.
Long before Judas betrayed Jesus with a kiss, something had already captured his heart.
Sin almost never starts with rebellion.
It usually starts with influence.
Scripture says in Proverbs 13:20:
"Whoever walks with the wise becomes wise, but the companion of fools will suffer harm."
The Hebrew reads:
הוֹלֵךְ אֶת־חֲכָמִים יֶחְכָּם וְרֹעֶה כְסִילִים יֵרוֹעַ
Holekh et-ḥakhamim yeḥkam, ve-ro'eh kesilim yeroa.
The word חֲכָמִים (ḥakhamim) means more than intelligent people.
It describes those who live skillfully under God's wisdom.
The word יֶחְכָּם (yeḥkam) means "will become wise."
Wisdom is contagious.
So is foolishness.
You eventually become like those you continually admire.
That truth should humble every one of us.
Because influence is not limited to the people sitting beside us.
Today, some of our closest influences have never met us.
They live inside our phones.
They speak through earbuds.
They entertain us through screens.
They shape our emotions before we even realize they have shaped our theology.
The enemy understands something many Christians forget:
Capture attention...
and eventually you capture affection.
Capture affection...
and eventually you influence worship.
That is why Paul urges believers in Romans 12:2:
"Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind..."
The Greek says:
καὶ μὴ συσχηματίζεσθε τῷ αἰῶνι τούτῳ
Kai mē syschēmatizesthe tō aiōni toutō.
The verb συσχηματίζεσθε (syschēmatizesthe) means:
"Do not allow yourselves to be molded according to the surrounding pattern."
Notice something remarkable.
Paul does not merely command believers to avoid obvious evil.
He warns against slowly taking the shape of a culture that does not belong to Christ.
The world rarely asks you to reject Jesus immediately.
It simply asks you to love Him a little less each day.
The devil knows that tiny compromises repeated over time often accomplish what open persecution never could.
This is why Jesus spoke so often about the heart.
Everything eventually flows from what we treasure.
Our influences slowly become our values.
Our values become our habits.
Our habits become our character.
Our character shapes our destiny.
King Solomon understood this deeply.
After receiving extraordinary wisdom from God, he gradually surrounded himself with influences that opposed God's commands.
The tragedy wasn't immediate.
It unfolded slowly.
Foreign relationships introduced foreign worship.
Foreign worship produced divided loyalty.
Divided loyalty eventually led an entire nation into idolatry.
The strongest believer is never stronger than the influences they continually embrace.
Even Peter—who boldly confessed Jesus as the Messiah—allowed human thinking to influence him.
When Peter rebuked Jesus for speaking about the cross, Jesus responded with startling words:
"Get behind Me, Satan!" (Matthew 16:23)
Peter wasn't possessed.
He was temporarily thinking according to human priorities rather than God's.
Jesus exposed the source behind the influence.
Not every attractive idea originates with God.
That truth remains just as urgent today.
Some voices make sin sound compassionate.
Others make compromise sound wise.
Some redefine love by removing truth.
Others redefine truth by removing love.
The Christian must test every influence against God's Word.
Not against popularity.
Not against emotion.
Not against celebrity.
Not against trends.
John writes:
Biblical discernment is not cynicism.
It is spiritual maturity.
Discernment asks one question above all others:
Does this voice make me love Jesus more?
Does it increase my hunger for holiness?
Does it deepen my reverence for Scripture?
Does it produce repentance?
Does it magnify Christ?
Or does it magnify self?
Because whatever consistently magnifies self eventually minimizes the Savior.
Jesus Himself declared:
"My sheep hear My voice, and I know them, and they follow Me." (John 10:27)
The Greek phrase is striking:
τὰ πρόβατα τῆς φωνῆς μου ἀκούουσιν
Ta probata tēs phōnēs mou akouousin.
Literally:
"My sheep keep listening to My voice."
Not once.
Continually.
Following Christ has always required recognizing His voice above every competing influence.
That becomes increasingly difficult when our lives are saturated with voices that rarely point us toward Him.
The frightening reality is that many believers spend far more time absorbing culture than absorbing Scripture.
Far more time scrolling than praying.
Far more time consuming opinions than meditating on God's Word.
Then we wonder why our spiritual appetite changes.
Whatever consistently feeds you eventually forms you.
This is why David declared:
"Your word I have treasured in my heart, that I might not sin against You." (Psalm 119:11)
The Hebrew word צָפַן (tsaphan) means to hide, treasure, store up, or preserve something precious.
God's Word is not meant to visit our minds occasionally.
It is meant to live within us continually.
The beautiful news of the Gospel is that Jesus does not merely warn us about harmful influences.
He transforms us despite them.
Every one of us has been shaped by sinful voices.
Some were wounded by abusive homes.
Some learned fear instead of faith.
Some absorbed bitterness.
Some inherited pride.
Some believed lies about identity.
Some listened to shame for years.
Others followed the applause of the world until they discovered it could never satisfy the soul.
Yet Jesus enters every broken story with astonishing grace.
He does not merely erase our past.
He redeems it.
He does not simply forgive sinners.
He adopts them.
He does not simply rescue failures.
He transforms them into witnesses.
The Gospel is the greatest reversal in human history.
Saul became Paul.
Peter the denier became Peter the preacher.
The woman caught in adultery became a testimony of mercy.
The thief on the cross entered Paradise through grace alone.
This is why our ministry continues proclaiming one unchanging truth:
No influence is greater than the transforming power of Jesus Christ.
No past is stronger than His cross.
No deception is beyond His truth.
No shame is beyond His mercy.
No sinner is beyond His invitation to repent and believe.
Perhaps today the Holy Spirit has quietly revealed influences that have been pulling your heart away from Christ.
Do not ignore His conviction.
Conviction is not condemnation.
It is the loving voice of the Good Shepherd calling His sheep back home.
Sometimes the most loving thing we can do is place God's truth where someone can encounter it.
Because one faithful voice surrendered to Christ can echo into generations you may never meet.
